teaser: A green nose, a blue hat, and one word from a critic that named a whole movement.

lesson.text: “Donatello among the wild beasts!” The critic Louis Vauxcelles said it in Paris in October 1905, then printed it in his newspaper. He was standing in a room of blazing paintings, in the middle of which someone had placed a polite, old-fashioned statue. Donatello was a gentle sculptor of the 1400s. The wild beasts, “les fauves” in French, were the painters.

The picture that drew the most laughter in that room was this one. Visitors pointed at it. Some reportedly tried to scratch the paint. It shows Amélie Matisse, the painter's wife, dressed up to go out: big hat, gloves, a fan. Nothing shocking in the subject. The outrage was entirely about color.

Henri Matisse was 35 and not a young rebel. He had trained for years, copied old paintings in the Louvre, and had a family to feed. He had just spent the summer of 1905 in Collioure, a fishing port in the south of France, painting side by side with his friend André Derain under a hard Mediterranean light. Something came loose there.

Matisse came to art late and by accident. He was a law clerk of about twenty, stuck in bed after an operation for appendicitis, when his mother brought him a box of paints to pass the time. He later said that from the moment he held it, he knew this was his life.

Back in Paris, he painted Amélie quickly, just before the exhibition opened. Painters had always used color to copy what they saw: pink for skin, brown for shadow. Matisse cut that link. Search her face for the place where the break is most brutal.
On a normal portrait, the shadow down the side of a nose is a soft brown. What did Matisse put there instead? Tap it.

spots.title: A green nose
spots.text: A stripe of pure green runs down the nose, with more green on the forehead and jaw. Next to the pink and yellow of the cheek, it still reads as shadow. The color is wrong and the face works.

lesson.text: Why does it work? Because green and pink-red are opposites, what painters call complementary colors: placed side by side, each makes the other look stronger. Matisse builds the head with these clashes, cool against warm, where earlier painters used dark against light. He draws with color.
Fauvism frees color from its job of describing things. A color is chosen for what it does next to its neighbors and for the feeling it carries, not because the object “is” that color.

People tell that Amélie actually posed in black. When someone asked Matisse what color her dress had really been, he is said to have answered: “Black, of course.” True or not, the story says it well: every color here was invented.

The hat deserves its place in the title. Amélie knew hats: for several years she had run a hat shop in Paris, and its income kept the family going while nobody bought Henri's pictures. So this towering pile of feathers and flowers is also a quiet tribute to the person who paid the rent.

spots.title: The hat
spots.text: A heap of blue, violet, orange and green strokes. You cannot name a single flower or feather, yet you understand at once: an enormous, fashionable hat.

spots.title: An orange neck
spots.text: Her neck is a band of flat orange and red. It works like a hinge of heat between the cool face and the cool dress.

spots.title: The fan
spots.text: White, pink and lilac dabs, laid on fast with a loaded brush. The fan is suggested, never outlined. Her gloved hand below it is a few green and violet patches.

spots.title: No room, no wall
spots.text: Behind her there is no place at all, only fields of pink, green and violet. The background is treated exactly like the figure: as color.

spots.title: The signature
spots.text: Matisse signs in the same green he used on her face. Around it the paint is thin and scrubbed, and the pale canvas shows through in places.

spots.title: Her eyes
spots.text: Dark, steady, a little tired, under strong arched brows. In the middle of the storm of paint, her look is calm and perfectly readable.

lesson.text: You may have noticed how unfinished it all looks. That was the second scandal. In 1905 a picture shown in public was supposed to be worked up and smooth. Matisse stops as soon as the colors balance, leaving strokes open and edges ragged. For many visitors this was simply a sketch that someone had dared to frame.

Matisse was badly hurt by the mockery. Then a telegram arrived: someone wanted to buy the painting. The buyers were Leo and Gertrude Stein, an American brother and sister living in Paris. They paid 500 francs, hung it in their apartment, and invited everyone they knew to come and argue about it. One of the guests was a young Spaniard named Pablo Picasso.

The painting followed the Stein family to California, which is why this scandal of the Paris art world now lives in San Francisco. It was later bought by the collector Elise Haas, who left it to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art.

Vauxcelles meant “wild beasts” as an insult. The painters kept it as their name. Within a few years, strong color chosen freely had stopped being a scandal and become one of the basic tools of modern art.

quiz.question: Where does the name “Fauves” come from?
options: A village where the painters worked
A critic's mocking remark about “wild beasts”
quiz.explanation: Louis Vauxcelles joked about a statue standing “among the wild beasts”, and the name stuck.

quiz.question: Who is the woman in the painting?
quiz.explanation: Matisse painted his wife Amélie, dressed to go out.

quiz.question: What color does Matisse use for the shadow on the nose?
quiz.explanation: A stripe of pure green stands in for the shadow.

quiz.question: Who bought the painting after the exhibition?
quiz.explanation: The American brother and sister paid 500 francs and hung it in their Paris apartment.

quiz.question: Why was the hat a meaningful subject for the couple?
options: Amélie had run a hat shop that supported the family
The hat was a gift from the Steins
quiz.explanation: Her shop's income kept the family going while his paintings did not sell.

facts.text: Matisse discovered painting as a child prodigy.
facts.explanation: He began at about twenty, when his mother gave him paints during an illness.

facts.text: Complementary colors placed side by side make each other look stronger.
facts.explanation: That is why the green shadow and the pink cheek work together.

facts.text: The painting was praised by the public when first shown in 1905.
facts.explanation: Visitors laughed at it and found it unfinished.
